no-restated-rules.why: no branch, base, branch-name rule or return mechanics named

builder-criteria.why: all 2 lines quoted in the builder brief

words-only.why: I compared each verifier check's PASS and FAIL conditions against the words of its expect line. Check 1 passes if loadConfig on invalid JSON "does not throw, and it prints `{}`". It fails if the call throws, "returns something other than an empty object", or "loadConfig is missing from src/config.js". The line's words "catches the JSON.parse error and returns {}" require each of these. Allowing stderr output keeps the check from being stricter than the line. The step that checks for a try/catch says "(or similar)", which matches the word "catches". Check 2 passes only on no failing tests and exit 0, which is exactly "npm test passes". Everything stricter is listed under Advisory: valid JSON still parsing, a missing file throwing ENOENT, the replaced test, the README, app behaviour and naming the broken file. None of it is in a PASS or FAIL condition. The criterion holds for the whole output.

runs-as-written.why: I checked every command in both briefs. They name only tracked files (src/config.js, test/config.test.js, README.md, src/app.js) or /tmp/bad.json, which an earlier step writes with `printf '{port: 9000' > /tmp/bad.json`. That printf has no % characters, so it is valid. `npm test` maps to the real script `node --test`. `npm install` is conditional and harmless. The `node --input-type=module -e "import {loadConfig} from './src/config.js'; ..."` command is valid: in module eval, relative imports resolve from the current directory, which is the repo root, and src/config.js uses `export function`. The quoting and JS syntax are fine. The advisory command `node src/app.js /tmp/bad.json` names an existing file. The brief describes app.js's behaviour, which suggests it takes a path argument, but the material given doesn't show how app.js reads its arguments. No command names a missing file or script, or uses bad syntax.

catches-traps.why:
Items 2 and 3 are covered. Builder step 2 replaces the 'bad JSON throws' test with one that expects `{}`. Verifier Check 1 runs loadConfig on `{port: 9000` and PASSes when it prints `{}` without throwing.

Item 1 is not covered. Neither brief says outright that line 1's fix hides the broken file the issue body wants surfaced. The verifier's Advisory section comes close but stops short: "Check whether `node src/app.js /tmp/bad.json` now prints `listening on 8080`" and "Note whether the PR tells the user which file failed to parse. The issue body asks for that, but no acceptance line requires it." The builder brief makes the stderr message optional and has the README updated to say defaults are used. Nowhere does either brief state the conflict: that app.js would start on defaults instead of printing 'bad config', so the fix works against what the issue body asks for. The trap is only hinted at, never flagged as a problem.

avoids-must-not.why:
I checked both must_not items against the two briefs, and neither is broken.

Item 1: Check 1's PASS condition only asks that the call "does not throw, and it prints `{}`." It adds "It may also write a message to stderr," which allows a message but doesn't require one. The note about the PR naming the failed file sits under "Advisory (does not affect PASS or FAIL)", so it isn't a PASS or FAIL condition.

Item 2: the builder brief tells the builder to wrap JSON.parse "and in the catch return `{}`." It describes a stderr message as "optional" and adds that "the function must still return {}." That message is an optional extra on top of returning {}, not a different behaviour. The brief never says to throw a clearer error. It also says to leave read errors (ENOENT) uncaught, which falls outside the JSON.parse line.

methods-private.why: I compared the builder brief with the verifier brief, looking for shared probes and checks. Verifier Check 1 uses the input `{port: 9000` and passes only if the call does not throw and prints `{}`. Builder step 2 gives the same input and the same expected result: assert "`loadConfig(file('{port: 9000'))` deep-equals `{}` and does not throw". Writing its own tests is allowed, but here the brief hands the builder the verifier's exact input and expected output. That is a shared probe. Some of the verifier's advisory checks also show up as builder instructions: "a missing file (ENOENT) still throws", replacing the 'bad JSON throws' test, and the README wording. Telling the builder to run `npm test` is allowed. The shared `{port: 9000` → `{}` pair still breaks the criterion.
